claim: Overview claim for koi.
sourceTypeNeeded: Species account with origin, domestication status and lifespan
plannedValue: Koi are domesticated colour forms of the Amur carp (Cyprinus rubrofuscus), a hardy river and pond fish of East Asia developed over centuries of ornamental breeding in Japan and China and now kept in garden ponds worldwide. They are pond fish rather than tropical aquarium fish: hardy across a wide temperature swing, active in summer warmth and slowing to near dormancy under winter ice, and long-lived - commonly 25 to 50 years with reports of more.
uncertainty: Taxonomy: commonly sold under the synonym Cyprinus carpio while ornamental strains trace to Cyprinus rubrofuscus (TankBud), matching the record's scientificName. Lifespan figures (25-50 years, occasionally more) come from PetMD.
notes: Maps to natural_distribution (overview).

claim: Adult size and growth claim for koi.
sourceTypeNeeded: Source giving typical and maximum adult length for koi
plannedValue: Adults commonly reach 60 cm, with PetMD listing up to 3 feet (about 90 cm) and AquariumLab expecting 24 to 36 inches (60-91 cm) - so plan every enclosure for the record's 90 cm figure from day one. Koi grow fast while young and live 25 to 50 years, so undersized systems fail quickly. Pair the adult size with the per-fish volume rule (about 250 gallons/950 L per large adult in a group) when stocking.
uncertainty: Typical adult size spans sources: TankBud 60 cm, PetMD up to 3 feet (~90 cm), AquariumLab 24-36 inches (60-91 cm). TankBud notes '60 cm or more in a large pond'. Growth rate per year not sourced. The record's sizeCm=90 sits at the top of the typical band.
notes: Existing sizeCm=90 consistent with the upper end of sources; no correction emitted (sizeCm outside the allowed correction set).

claim: Tank requirements claim for koi, including jump and lid callout.
sourceTypeNeeded: Husbandry guides stating enclosure scale, filtration, cycling and cover for koi
plannedValue: Koi are pond fish: one koi needs roughly 1,000 L to start, and a group needs a pond of several thousand litres with strong filtration (filter turning the volume over at least twice an hour). Run it cycled - never add koi to an uncycled tank - with slow water circulation and aeration that is not optional. Cover the water: koi jump 60-90 cm under stress, so fit netting or a secure lid with an air gap for gas exchange, and keep the temperature in the 15-25 C comfort band.
uncertainty: Parameter sources disagree on comfort ranges (TankBud 4-27 C / pH 7.0-8.5, AquariumLab 15-25 C / pH 7.0-8.5, PetMD 18-24 C / pH 7.0-8.6); corrections were emitted only for temperature (see temp claims). No ph correction claim was emitted because no ph_range gap is registered for this record, but the record's phMin=6.5 sits below every sourced low (6.8 LiveAquaria, 7.0 TankBud/AquariumLab) - flagged for separate review.
notes: Jump callout mandatory in this destination. Difficulty conflict flagged in body:practicalVerdict.

claim: Footprint claim for koi (volume != footprint).
sourceTypeNeeded: Source explicitly framing koi housing as length/width/surface area rather than litres
plannedValue: Read the 1,000 L minimum as floor area first: koi swim side to side, so a long, wide, moderately deep enclosure (on the order of 2.4 x 1 m of floor) beats a tall column, because a 60-90 cm fish turns at the ends of a straight lane. Keep the lane clear of hardscape, judge stocking by surface area rather than volume, and remember a narrow tank can hit the litre target while leaving the fish nowhere to turn.
uncertainty: The 240 x 100 cm floor is our derivation from the 1,000 L minimum; only AquariumLab's qualitative long-over-tall rule and the six-foot example are sourced. LiveAquaria adds a surface-area stocking rule (about one inch of fish per square foot) seen in search results only.
notes: Addresses CRITICAL safety gap adult_footprint; derivation must be published with the figure.

claim: Behavior claim for koi.
sourceTypeNeeded: Source describing koi social behaviour and feeding habits
plannedValue: Koi are peaceful, social pond fish that live in schools, learn to recognise their keepers and will take food from the hand. They root through soft substrate, uproot plants and swallow anything small enough. They cope with a very wide temperature swing - active in summer, near-dormant under winter ice - and when they jump it is a stress response (poor water quality, predators, spawning chases), not play, so repeated jumping means test the water first.
uncertainty: Territoriality itself is not documented in any fetched source, so no territorial flag is claimed; the passage describes sociability, feeding behaviour and jumping-as-stress instead (jump evidence from KoiQuanta).
notes: Corroborated by PetMD (peaceful, social, thrive in schools) and KoiQuanta (jumping is a stress behaviour).

claim: Feeding claim for koi.
sourceTypeNeeded: Source describing koi diet composition and feeding schedule
plannedValue: Omnivore: feed a varied, koi-formulated diet - sinking pellets with greens and occasional live or frozen foods (TankBud). Give small portions eaten within a couple of minutes and scale to temperature: below about 13 C feed every few days, once daily around 13-21 C, twice daily above 21 C (PetMD), and withdraw food entirely at around 10 C when metabolism shuts down (K.O.I.). Remove leftovers daily; uneaten food fouls the water.
uncertainty: Exact protein/carbohydrate ratios and feed quantities per kg of fish are not sourced. Temperature-driven feeding rules differ slightly between sources (PetMD 55/70 F thresholds vs AquariumLab 65 F protein switch vs K.O.I. withdrawal at ~10 C).
notes: Existing diet=Omnivore matches sources; no correction emitted.

claim: Compatibility claim for koi.
sourceTypeNeeded: Husbandry source stating koi tankmate rules
plannedValue: Keep koi with other large, robust pond fish only: goldfish (single-tailed varieties preferred), other koi, or cool-tolerant community fish. Anything small enough to swallow is food, plants get uprooted and small invertebrates are eaten. Do not overcrowd - overcrowded ponds lead to stress and disease (PetMD) - and treat 'at least five' as the social minimum, not a stocking target: volume and filtration set the real ceiling.
uncertainty: Named tankmates limited to goldfish/other koi; PetMD's temperature-tolerance rule (64-75 F) is the practical filter for anything else. Quarantine guidance (four to six weeks for new fish) comes from PetMD.
notes: Do not generate an incompatibleSpecies list from this evidence; relation destinations are out of scope for Stage A.

claim: Practical verdict claim for koi.
sourceTypeNeeded: Husbandry sources covering enclosure scale, filtration, cycling and difficulty rating
plannedValue: Verdict: a 1,000-litre-plus pond commitment, not a beginner aquarium fish. Koi produce heavy waste, so budget for powerful filtration, weekly water changes, mandatory aeration and a fully cycled system before any fish arrives. Cover the water because they jump under stress, keep them in a school of at least five with room to cruise a straight lane, and feed a varied formulated diet scaled to temperature. The reward is a social, hand-taming, 60-90 cm fish that lives 25-50 years; the cost is decades of filtration, water changes and pond-scale maintenance - PetMD rates the care 'Intermediate to advanced' even though this record says Beginner.
uncertainty: Difficulty ratings conflict across sources and with the record: record Beginner, LiveAquaria 'Easy', TankBud 'Medium', PetMD 'Intermediate to advanced'. The difficulty field is outside the Stage A correction set, so the conflict is flagged here only and no difficulty correction claim is emitted.
notes: Blunt verdict per spec; difficulty conflict and jump callout included.

claim: Overview claim for alligator gar.
sourceTypeNeeded: Species account with range, ecology and conservation status
plannedValue: The alligator gar (Atractosteus spatula) is a living fossil from the lower Mississippi basin and Gulf Coast states of the south-eastern USA and northern/central Mexico - the largest exclusively freshwater fish in North America, essentially unchanged for roughly 100 million years. It occurs in large lakes, rivers, sluggish tributaries and backwaters, tolerates fresh and brackish water, and reaches a recorded 3.05 m with wild fish routinely aged past 50 years. Several US states restrict private possession, so check local regulations before acquiring one.
uncertainty: Habitat detail from the same source: large lakes and rivers to sluggish tributaries, backwaters and pools; fresh and brackish with a preference for large rivers with extensive floodplains; 'Does not tend to inhabit swiftly-flowing environments.' Legal status varies by US state (FishStores) - verify local regulations separately.
notes: Maps to natural_distribution (overview). 'Living fossil'/100-million-year framing corroborated by FishStores.

claim: Adult size and growth claim for alligator gar.
sourceTypeNeeded: Source giving typical and maximum adult length plus growth rate
plannedValue: Adults reach 180-240 cm (6-8 ft) typically, with a scientific record of 305 cm and historic accounts beyond 3 m. Growth is relentless - 45-60 cm in year one, about 90 cm by year two, 120-150 cm by year four - and there is no plateau: the fish keeps growing for decades, so 'it will only grow as big as its tank' is a myth that produces kinked spines and organ failure. Plan for 2-3 m from day one; captive lifespan is 15-40 years with good housing, wild fish live 50-95+ years.
uncertainty: Record sizeCm=150 is below every sourced adult figure: FishStores 180-240 cm typical (up to 10 ft historically), Guidarium 200 cm, SeriouslyFish 305 cm recorded maximum. sizeCm is outside the Stage A correction set, so the mismatch is flagged here for separate review only. Captive-vs-wild growth differs; the record's size is best read as a subadult figure.

claim: Tank requirements claim for alligator gar, including jump and lid callout.
sourceTypeNeeded: Husbandry guides stating enclosure scale, construction, lid and cycling for alligator gar
plannedValue: This is not a home-aquarium fish. A juvenile can start in about 680 L (180 gal) up to roughly 75 cm, but adults need an indoor pond or stock tank of at least 305 x 152 x 91 cm (~4,164 L), with published alternatives up to 400 cm / 8,000 L. Build in pond-rated EPDM or fiberglass (ordinary pool liners puncture), floor-load the weight (over 7,500 kg for 2,000 L - consult a structural engineer), and fit a cover that stops jumps while leaving the surface open, because the fish gulps air every 5-30 minutes and a tightly sealed top will suffocate it. Cycle for 6-10 weeks before purchase, target 4-6x hourly turnover, and keep nitrate below 30 ppm.

claim: Footprint claim for alligator gar (volume != footprint).
sourceTypeNeeded: Source framing enclosure requirements as length/width rather than litres
plannedValue: Read any volume minimum as floor area first: a gar must be able to fully extend, pivot and turn without scraping snout or spine. The published practical floor is about 305 x 152 cm of open floor with 91 cm of depth, and wider is better (the FAQ says at least 4 to 5 feet across). A too-short tank is not a comfort problem - it produces the species' most common chronic injury, permanent spinal misalignment from collisions with the walls, because a startled gar accelerates faster than the box is long.

claim: Behavior claim for alligator gar.
sourceTypeNeeded: Sources describing temperament, social behaviour and feeding behaviour of alligator gar
plannedValue: The alligator gar is an apex ambush predator: motionless near the surface like a floating log until prey is within reach, then a burst fast enough to cause collisions in short tanks. It is not community-safe by diet rather than by aggression - anything mouth-sized is eaten, so tankmate safety is a gape measurement taken every six months, not a species list. Conspecifics are tolerated only in very large enclosures where each fish has clear personal space, and feeding-time collisions between them are brief but violent. Provide floating cover over open water so the fish feels secure at the surface, and expect a jumper that will test any lid.
uncertainty: Temperament label itself is disputed (see temperament claim, PENDING_RESEARCH); conspecific tolerance is also disputed (SF 'kept alone' vs FishStores/Guidarium allowance for groups in very large systems). Territoriality toward tankmates is not documented - exclusion is by predation and space, not declared territory.
notes: Behaviour synthesised from SF (ambush, alone, air-breathing) and FishStores (gape rule, conspecific space, feeding collisions); Guidarium adds jumper/hyperactive traits.

claim: Feeding claim for alligator gar.
sourceTypeNeeded: Sources describing diet composition and feeding schedule for alligator gar
plannedValue: Obligate piscivore: whole prey items only - rotating tilapia, silversides/smelt, shell-on shrimp, squid and earthworms, with a weekly vitamin B1 supplement. Never feed mammal meat (beef heart, chicken) and never build the diet on feeder goldfish or rosy reds: thiaminase destroys vitamin B1 and the damage is cumulative and irreversible, plus feeders carry parasites and disease. Feed juveniles daily, sub-adults every other day, and adults two to three times a week (SeriouslyFish says one to two meals at most); remove leftovers and keep body condition lean - fatty liver is the common overfeeding error. Transition wild-caught fish onto frozen foods with the stick-and-jiggle method rather than live feeders.
uncertainty: Schedule differs slightly between sources: FishStores juveniles daily, sub-adults every other day, adults 2-3x per week; SeriouslyFish juveniles daily, adults 1-2 meals per week at most. Both agree adults are fed sparingly. Thiaminase/feeder-fish warnings are unanimous.
notes: Existing diet field not corrected; no diet conflict with sources (carnivore/piscivore consistent).

claim: Compatibility claim for alligator gar.
sourceTypeNeeded: Husbandry sources stating tankmate rules for alligator gar
plannedValue: Default: keep it alone (SeriouslyFish). In genuinely massive systems, tankmates must pass two tests - physically impossible to swallow, and able to tolerate the same enormous enclosure. The named candidates are large arowana, freshwater stingrays, assertive large cichlids and redtail catfish in 3,000-plus gallon setups. Re-measure the gar's gape every six months; when in doubt, rehome the smaller fish before it disappears. Common mistakes: plecos (swallowed whole or attached to the gar's slime coat) and anything small enough to be eaten during night feeding.
uncertainty: SeriouslyFish is stricter ('not a community fish'; 'Best kept alone'); FishStores names conditional companions for 3,000+ gallon systems (silver/Asian arowana, freshwater stingrays, large central American cichlids, redtail catfish) with a six-monthly gape check. No source lists invertebrates as safe.

claim: Practical verdict claim for alligator gar.
sourceTypeNeeded: Husbandry sources covering enclosure scale, filtration, lifespan and rehoming reality
plannedValue: Verdict: expert-only, build-first commitment. Budget a custom indoor pond or vat of at least 305 x 152 cm and 4,000+ litres (published figures run to 8,000 L), pond-grade filtration with 4-6x turnover, weekly 30-50% water changes, a six-to-ten-week fishless cycle started before you buy anything, and a cover that stops jumps without blocking air. The animal is a 2-3 m predator that grows for 50-95 years, eats whole prey, and will outgrow your house if you let it. Have a written rehoming plan (two backup homes and a tank-buster fund) and check your state's possession laws before purchase: public aquariums are full and dumping a non-native gar is both illegal and ecologically catastrophic. Skip it and keep a Florida gar if you cannot commit to all of that.
uncertainty: Difficulty conflict: record says Advanced while FishStores says 'Expert only' and marks the species for experienced monster-fish keepers; difficulty is outside the Stage A correction set so the conflict is flagged here only. Rehoming and legal constraints are US-specific.
notes: Blunt verdict per spec; jump callout included via lid/cover clause; difficulty mismatch recorded in uncertainty.

claim: The overview section presents the redtail catfish as a giant Amazon/Orinoco pimelodid reaching 135 cm that is a documented aquarium-trade size trap.
sourceTypeNeeded: SCIENTIFIC_LITERATURE
source: FishBase - Phractocephalus hemioliopterus (Redtail catfish) species summary
plannedValue: Phractocephalus hemioliopterus is a giant long-whiskered catfish of the Amazon and Orinoco basins, inhabiting everything from rapids to flooded forest across much of northern South America. FishBase records a maximum of 135 cm TL and 44.2 kg, making it one of the largest catfishes ever offered in the aquarium trade. It is sold cheaply as a 5 cm juvenile, and Seriously Fish documents the consequences: public aquaria saturated with donated adults and feral populations established by dumped fish in the USA and several other countries. Both FishBase and specialist references treat it as an expert or public-aquarium species rather than a home-tank fish.
notes: Distribution/habitat corroboration from Seriously Fish (Amazon and Rio Orinoco basins) and FishBase.

claim: The growth section states a realistic captive adult of roughly 100-130 cm, explosive juvenile growth, and maturity at about 85 cm TL.
sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE
source: Aquarist Atlas - Redtail Catfish (Phractocephalus hemioliopterus) Size & Care
plannedValue: Expect a typical captive adult of roughly 100-130 cm (3-4 ft) and tens of kilograms; FishBase's maximum is 135 cm TL, while its common wild length is only 60 cm TL, so hobby fish grown in good space approach the top of the range. Growth is explosive during the first years - Aquarist Atlas reports roughly 1-2 inches (2.5-5 cm) per month - and sexual maturity does not arrive until about 85 cm TL, at which point the fish already exceeds virtually all home aquariums. The largest recorded specimen measured 134 cm and weighed over 40 kg. With proper housing the species lives 15-20 years or more.
notes: Maturity figure from FishBase ('Maturity: Lm ? range 85 - ? cm') and Aquarist Atlas (~85 cm TL); lifespan 15-20+ years per Pet Zone Tropical Fish.

claim: The tank requirements section specifies 360 x 240 x 120 cm minimum, sump-scale filtration, dim lighting and sand or bare bottom.
sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE
source: Seriously Fish - Phractocephalus hemioliopterus (Red-tail Catfish) species profile
plannedValue: For a single adult, Seriously Fish gives an absolute minimum of 360 x 240 x 120 cm (about 10,368 litres), and Aquarist Atlas independently repeats the same 360 x 240 in footprint. Filtration must be sump- or pond-scale because a 44 kg carnivore produces what Aquarist Atlas calls a 'commensurate bioload'. Keep the lighting dim with only large, anchored pieces of bogwood or smooth rock - or no decor at all - and use bare bottom or fine sand, since gravel can be swallowed or jam in the gills. ScotCat notes that height matters little (18-24 in is ample) but the tank must be at least 8 ft long with roughly 36 in of width so the fish can turn.
notes: Substrate guidance corroborated by ScotCat (gravel moved, subdued light, caves/branches) and Aquarist Atlas (scaleless skin).

claim: The footprint section explains that floor length, not tank volume or height, is what a 1.2-1.3 m catfish needs.
sourceTypeNeeded: COMMUNITY_SUPPLEMENTARY
source: Pet Zone Tropical Fish - Redtail Catfish care guide
plannedValue: Volume is the wrong metric here: what the fish needs is floor. A 1.2-1.3 m predator must be able to turn and cruise, which is why Seriously Fish specifies a 360 x 240 cm base even for its 'absolute minimum', and ScotCat still insists on an 8 ft tank about 36 in wide 'so that it can turn comfortly'. Pet Zone Tropical Fish reduces the principle to 'Length > Depth > Height: They need floor space more than vertical space'. A 500-litre tank of any height fails this test because its length is typically under 150 cm.
notes: Corroborates the minTankLengthCm/minTankWidthCm structured claims.

claim: The behavior section describes a nocturnal, solitary, territorial predator with cave requirements that becomes destructive when cramped.
sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE
source: Aquarist Atlas - Redtail Catfish (Phractocephalus hemioliopterus) Size & Care
plannedValue: Redtails are nocturnal, gape-limited predators: Aquarist Atlas describes a 'nocturnal predator that requires large cave-like cover' that hunts mainly at night using its barbels. They are solitary and territorial with their own kind - Seriously Fish reports territoriality toward conspecifics and other large pimelodids, and ScotCat calls the fish 'definitely a loner' that will quickly kill tank mates. In cramped quarters they become stressed bulldozers, smashing heaters and shoving decor around. Despite their predatory nature they are famously personable, often begging for food like dogs, but friendliness never overrides the size of their mouth.
notes: Heater destruction corroborated by Seriously Fish ('A large specimen can easily destroy glass heaterstats'); begging behavior from Aquarist Atlas.

claim: The feeding section describes an opportunistic carnivore fed meaty foods 1-3 times weekly with strict overfeeding warnings.
sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE
source: Seriously Fish - Phractocephalus hemioliopterus (Red-tail Catfish) species profile
plannedValue: Diet is carnivorous and opportunistic: FishBase records adults feeding on 'fish, crabs and fruits', and Seriously Fish lists wild fish, invertebrates and fallen fruit. Offer varied meaty foods - prawns, mussels, earthworms, whitefish fillets and large sinking carnivore pellets - and avoid mammal meat and feeder fish, which Seriously Fish warns risk organ damage and disease introduction. Adults need at most 'a single meal per week' (Seriously Fish) or two to three sizeable meals (Aquarist Atlas), never daily portions. Overfeeding is a leading cause of death, and redtails swallow inedible objects, so keep small gravel and trinkets out of the tank.
notes: Diet confirmed as carnivore - no correction needed for existing diet=Carnivore (fruit intake is opportunistic, not a diet-class change).

claim: The compatibility section warns that any tankmate it can swallow will be eaten and names only giant tankmates as possible companions.
sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE
source: Aquarist Atlas - Redtail Catfish (Phractocephalus hemioliopterus) Size & Care
plannedValue: Compatibility turns entirely on mouth size: Aquarist Atlas states it 'will consume any tankmate it can engulf', so anything shorter than about half the catfish's length is food. At public-aquarium scale suitable companions exist - Seriously Fish suggests doradids such as Oxydoras niger or Pterodoras granulosus, plus very large characins and cyprinids in deep water. For ordinary keepers the honest answer is a single fish: ScotCat warns it 'would quickly kill any tank mates', and Seriously Fish says it should be the only large pimelodid present unless space is truly unlimited. Snails, shrimp and crabs should also be assumed edible.
notes: Prose names tankmate species relationships only as compatibility illustration; structured relationship fields are out of SPEC 11 scope.

sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE

If you cannot guarantee adult-sized housing for 15-20 years starting today, do not buy it.

claim: The overview section presents the zebra moray as the crustacean-specialist, fish-safe moray of the Indo-Pacific and eastern Pacific.
sourceTypeNeeded: SCIENTIFIC_LITERATURE
source: FishBase - Gymnomuraena zebra (Zebra moray) species summary
plannedValue: Gymnomuraena zebra is the sole member of its genus, a heavy-bodied, boldly banded moray with blunt molar-like teeth built for crushing shells. It is one of the widest-ranging morays on earth: FishBase records it across the Indo-West Pacific from the Red Sea and East Africa to the Society Islands, north to the Ryukyu and Hawaiian islands, south to the Great Barrier Reef, plus the eastern Pacific from southern Baja California to Colombia and the Galapagos, on reef-associated rocky and sandy bottoms from 3 to 50 m depth. FishBase puts maximum size at 150 cm TL with a common length of 50 cm TL, and lists it as Least Concern (IUCN). Its crustacean diet is what defines it in the hobby: unlike almost every other moray offered for sale, it eats hard-shelled invertebrates rather than fish, which is why specialist sources describe it as one of the few large morays that is generally safe around fish tankmates - Reef Builders calls it 'peaceful, hardy, adaptable, and generally safe around piscine tankmates', and Wet Web Media classes it among the 'few gentle morays'.
notes: Distribution and habitat from FishBase; characterization corroborated by Reef Builders and Wet Web Media.

Most specimens are unlikely to achieve that prodigious length.' Shape is non-negotiable: a standard flat-and-wide tank, never hex, octagon or show shapes. The interior must be built around rockwork - Reef Builders: 'it does require lots of rockwork to hide in' - with a dark cave, PVC pipe or covered pot so the eel can 'hide completely out of the light' (WWM). claim: The behavior section describes a reclusive, poor-eyed cave-dweller that is peaceful toward fish but bites careless hands.
sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE
source: Wet Web Media - The Zebra Moray Eel, Gymnomuraena zebra (Bob Fenner)
plannedValue: Zebra morays are reclusive, secretive cave-dwellers: Wet Web Media describes animals 'reclusive in the wild' that need to hide completely out of the light, FishBase calls the species 'a secretive inhabitant of sandy and rocky bottoms, crevices and ledges of seaward reefs', and Reef Builders notes it 'doesn’t need much in the way of open swimming space'. Activity is more flexible than the typical moray's - Wikipedia records nocturnal hunting while Reef Builders photographs show animals 'active during the day' - so expect activity at various times with hiding as the default posture. They hunt by smell with poor eyesight: WWM warns they 'have a great sense of olfaction, but unfortunately bad vision. Do not hand feed', and Reef Builders notes the eel 'may mistake your digits for something edible'. Toward fish they are remarkably gentle - 'Unlike other morays, the zebra rarely bites tankmates or aquarists when doing routine maintenance' (WWM) - but the jaw is built for crushing shells, so any hand in the rockwork risks a serious defensive bite.

claim: The feeding section describes an obligate crustacean-crusher fed meaty foods with tongs no more than twice weekly.
sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE
source: Reef Builders - Gymnomuraena zebra: Another Moray You Just Might Love! species profile
plannedValue: Obligate hard-shelled carnivore: FishBase - 'It feeds primarily on xanthid crabs, but also on other crustaceans, mollusks and sea urchins' - matches the 'blunt and molar-like' teeth designed 'for crushing hard-shelled prey items' described by Reef Builders, and Wikipedia likewise records a diet of 'crustaceans, sea urchins and mollusks'. In captivity offer varied meaty items - shrimp, clams, mussels, squid, crab - always with tongs or a feeding stick, never by hand: Reef Builders calls hand-feeding a mistake because the eel 'has notoriously poor eyesight and may mistake your digits for something edible', and WWM repeats 'Do not hand feed'. Frequency is low: 'Feed no more than twice weekly' (Reef Builders) or 'The smaller ones maybe twice a week, the larger specimens once' (WWM); WWM adds that overfeeding 'simply adds to water pollution and growth/size problems'. Reluctant or new eels can be enticed with live ghost shrimp and trained onto frozen food (Reef Builders, WWM). No fetched source describes a separate juvenile versus adult diet beyond portion size.

claim: The compatibility section names mouth-size as the only fish rule and all crustaceans and most invertebrates as forbidden.
sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE
source: Wet Web Media - The Zebra Moray Eel, Gymnomuraena zebra (Bob Fenner)
plannedValue: One rule governs fish: mouth-size. Wet Web Media - 'most all fishes are safe as long as they are more than mouth-size and your moray is regularly fed' - and Reef Builders - 'most fish will be fine with one', while still advising against 'bite-sized species as tankmates'. Invertebrates are the hard exclusion: WWM says the eel 'will eventually eat any and all crustaceans' and is 'too large and "clumsy" to be kept with most invertebrates, definitely not in reef set-ups'; Reef Builders agrees crustaceans must go and, although the eel 'won’t directly harm sessile invertebrates', still excludes it from most reef aquariums over waste production and toppling aquascaping. Other eels and non-crustacean livestock can work - WWM reports mixing 'many types with the zebra with impunity' - but watch triggers, puffers and other 'trouble-makers' that might pester a shy, poor-eyed animal, keep hands out of the rockwork, and never house the eel with anything it could swallow whole.

claim: The practical verdict section rates it an excellent but hidden fish-only specimen that fails reef, invert and nano contexts.
sourceTypeNeeded: SPECIALIST_REFERENCE
source: Wet Web Media - The Zebra Moray Eel, Gymnomuraena zebra (Bob Fenner)
plannedValue: Verdict: one of the best morays available, but only in the right system. Wet Web Media calls it 'an excellent, albeit hidden show aquarium specimen for fish-only marine systems' that is 'long-lasting, disease resistant, and companionable', supremely hardy, and documented for twenty-plus years. The demands are modest but non-negotiable: at least 100 gallons in a flat, standard tank (Reef Builders), dense rockwork with a dark cave, a completely tight cover, a protein skimmer with real circulation and aeration, monthly 20% water changes, no crustaceans anywhere in the display, and feeding only once or twice a week with tongs. It is a poor fit for reefs (rockwork toppling and waste), invertebrate displays, nano systems, and keepers who want an outgoing display fish - it will spend most of its time hidden. Accept a mostly hidden, peaceful, long-lived crustacean-eater in a covered fish-only tank and it is an easy recommendation; want visible activity or a reef, and pick something else.

claim: Feeding claim for clown knifefish.
sourceTypeNeeded: Sources describing diet and captive feeding for clown knives
plannedValue: Carnivore and active predator: clown knives will eagerly swallow any fish that fits in their mouth, and wild fish eat aquatic insects, mollusks, shrimps and small fishes. Get them onto pellets and dry foods early (many resist), then vary with earthworms, bloodworm and other meaty items, fed after the lights go out to match their nocturnal rhythm. Remove uneaten food in the morning - leftover food is water quality damage on a fish that is already extremely sensitive to poor conditions - and never use feeder goldfish or livebearers as food.

claim: Compatibility claim for clown knifefish.
sourceTypeNeeded: Sources stating tankmate rules and predation risk for clown knives
plannedValue: House it singly by default: two knifefish fight ferociously, and only very young specimens tolerate each other. Any tankmate must be far too large to swallow, because it is highly predatory with a deceptively large mouth - TFH's tankmates-eaten warning and Aqueon's swallow-anything rule are the same rule. Give any large catfish alternatives to the caves or they will compete for them, and add the knifefish last so you can watch how it settles. Juveniles are routinely sold into community tanks, where they eat everything and then stunt.

Tankmate lists differ by source: TheTropicalTank suggests large catfish, bichirs and Siamese tigerfish; Aqueon suggests silver dollars, tinfoil barbs, angelfish, large cichlids, larger gouramis and Synodontis - none of which survive a 100 cm adult's mouth.
notes: Used compat_warnings because community_suitability is absent from this record's requirements - explained here rather than skipped silently. Cross-links size_based_predation and groupSize.

claim: Practical verdict claim for clown knifefish.

plannedValue: Verdict: a common fish that most keepers should skip - TFH says so directly: one of those common species that shouldn't be, because very few aquarists can properly house these behemoths. Budget 200 gallons or more with a long footprint, caves, a secure cover, heavy filtration and a strict water-change routine for a scaleless, medication-sensitive fish that demands undetectable ammonia, plus a lifetime of meaty carnivore feeding. Keep it single, keep every tankmate too large to swallow, and buy it only if you can house a 120 cm nocturnal predator for the long term - the usual failure path is a cute 10 cm juvenile in a community tank that eats everything and then stunts.

claim: Overview claim for iridescent shark: distribution, status and trade context.
sourceTypeNeeded: Database species account covering distribution and status
plannedValue: The iridescent shark (Pangasianodon hypophthalmus), also sold as the Siamese shark, Sutchi catfish or Pangasius, is a large shark catfish native to the Mekong, Chao Phraya and Maeklong basins of Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam. Wild stocks are IUCN Endangered, but it is one of Asia's most important aquaculture species, which is why thousands of juveniles reach the aquarium trade every year - usually sold as 5-8 cm silvery-blue youngsters with almost no warning of what follows. It is a pelagic, open-water river fish that can live 20 years or more.
uncertainty: IUCN assessment dates from January 2011; the Endangered status refers to wild populations, and the species is mass-farmed, so trade fish are almost all aquaculture stock. Trade names (Sutchi catfish, Siamese shark, Pangasius) refer to the same fish.

claim: Adult size and growth claim for iridescent shark.

They can live 20 years or more, making this one of the longest commitments in the hobby. The profile's 100 cm must be planned for from the day a 5 cm juvenile is bought, because growth is relentless and the tank does not slow it - undersized housing produces a panicked, injured fish, not a small one.

Keep the tank dimly lit with low, secured hardscape, strong biological filtration and no narrow gaps where a panicked fish can wedge or injure itself.

claim: Behaviour claim for iridescent shark.
sourceTypeNeeded: Sources describing temperament, activity and social behaviour
plannedValue: Iridescent sharks are peaceful but nervous open-water swimmers with poor eyesight: startled, they dash chaotically and injure themselves on glass, decor and tankmates, which is why crumpled tanks kill them. They are not aggressive - they are easily intimidated by boisterous fish and will eat anything small enough to swallow - and they constantly cruise the middle water column, bothering sedentary tankmates simply by being busy. Young fish school; adults become more solitary but still want their own kind, so plan for company and space together.

claim: Feeding claim for iridescent shark.
sourceTypeNeeded: Sources describing natural and captive diet
plannedValue: Omnivore with an age-based shift: juveniles need a protein-rich diet (chopped earthworm, bloodworm, pellets) to develop correctly, while adults need a growing share of vegetable matter - spinach, peas, Spirulina foods and occasional fruit. In the wild they take fish, crustaceans and vegetable debris, and in old age they lose teeth and lean further toward vegetation. Feed small portions two to three times a day that are finished within 5-10 minutes, and do not let a greedy fish drive overfeeding - waste management is already the main maintenance load.
uncertainty: Feeding frequency figures come from Aquario (two to three times a day, only what is eaten in 5-10 minutes) and are not independently corroborated; live feeder fish are not endorsed by any source.

claim: Compatibility claim for iridescent shark.

plannedValue: Not aggressive, but three ways to fail: anything small enough to swallow is eaten, sedentary or shy fish are stressed by constant cruising, and aggressive or boisterous fish intimidate it into panicked, self-injury dashes. In genuinely huge systems the candidates are large, peaceful benthic and shoaling fish such as doradids, pacu or large cyprinids - all far too big to swallow. For most keepers that math does not work, which is why FishBase simply says not recommended for home aquariums: in practice this is a species-only fish.

Budget 20 years of heavy filtration, secured equipment, a heavy lid, open swimming space and a nervous 100-130 cm fish that injures itself when cramped - and remember that public aquaria are already inundated with cast-offs they cannot take.

claim: Behaviour claim for longnose gar.
sourceTypeNeeded: Sources describing hunting strategy, activity and social behaviour
source: Virginia Tech Virtual Aquarium: Longnose Gar
plannedValue: Longnose gars are sedentary ambush predators: they hang motionless near vegetation or float at the surface - where gulping air looks like basking - then explode forward in a sudden attack on passing fish. They are not documented as territorial aggressors; the real social problem is size, since anything not much larger than them is prey while larger active fish harass a sedentary gar in return. Expect a fish that uses the whole floor to turn, rests in open water rather than caves, and needs space to accelerate without hitting its snout.

claim: Feeding claim for longnose gar.

Young gar grow fast and waste away if underfed, so feed adequately while growing them out - but avoid feeder fish where possible (disease risk) and never rely on them as the whole diet.
